'''''Hedychium gardnerianum''''', the '''Kahili ginger, Kahila garland-lily''' or '''ginger lily''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the ginger [[family (botany)|family]] Zingiberaceae, native to the [[Himalayas]] in [[India]], [[Nepal]], and [[Bhutan]]. It is an erect [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] growing to {{convert|8 |ft|m|abbr=on}} tall with long, bright green leaves clasping the tall stems. The very fragrant pale yellow and red flowers are held in dense spikes above the foliage. They appear towards the end of summer.

==Cultivation==
''Hedychium gardnerianum'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] in gardens and parks. It prefers a warm tropical climate, although it can thrive in sub-tropical and temperate regions as it tolerates occasional frosts. In the [[UK]] it has been given the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web 
| url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/8427/i-Hedychium-gardnerianum-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Hedychium gardnerianum''
| access-date=3 March 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf 
| title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 46 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society 
| access-date = 2 March 2018}}</ref> It is best grown in a warm, sheltered spot where temperatures do not fall below freezing, and is given a deep mulch during the winter months. Alternatively it can be grown under glass in a well-lit conservatory or greenhouse.

==Invasive species==
The plant is a serious [[invasive species]] in certain areas. It is known as 'wild kahili ginger' and is listed as a weed of concern on conservation land in [[New Zealand]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/kahili-ginger|title=Kahili ginger|access-date=23 April 2009|publisher=Biosecurity New Zealand, [[New Zealand Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry]]|year=2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150122215049/http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/kahili-ginger|archive-date=22 January 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Hawaii]],<ref name="hi">{{Cite web|url=http://www.state.hi.us/dlnr/dofaw/hortweeds/species/hedgar.htm |title=Hawaii's Most Invasive Horticultural Plants – kahili ginger |access-date=September 24, 2007 |publisher=State of Hawaii – Department of Land and Natural Resources |year=2007 |author=State of Hawaii – Department of Land and Natural Resources |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070926234511/http://www.state.hi.us/dlnr/dofaw/hortweeds/species/hedgar.htm |archive-date=September 26, 2007 }}</ref> [[South Africa]]<ref name=invasives-ZA>{{cite web | url=https://invasives.org.za/fact-sheet/kahili-ginger-lily/ | title=Kahili ginger lily – Invasive Species South Africa }}</ref> and the [[Azores]].<ref name="az">{{Cite web|url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/distribution_detail.asp?si=57&di=26608&sts=sss&lang=EN|title=Details of this species in Azores|access-date=January 31, 2011|publisher=Global Invasive Species Database|year=2004|author=Invasive Species Specialist Group|archive-date=March 4, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304110652/http://www.issg.org/database/species/distribution_detail.asp?si=57&di=26608&sts=sss&lang=EN|url-status=dead}}</ref>

It has been recognized as one of "[[100 of the World's Worst Invasive Alien Species]]" by the [[IUCN]] [[Invasive Species Specialist Group]] (ISSG).

==Control as a weed==
In areas where ''Hedychium gardnerianum'' is not of a concern, it may still require control depending on the environment, and its potential as an invasive species in the long term. The simplest way to reduce spread is monitoring. Removal of flower heads before they set seed, and monitoring spread of the [[rhizomes]] in these situations will enable ''Hedychium gardnerianum'' to be managed in cooler temperate climates such as in the [[United Kingdom]].

In [[tropical climate|tropical]], or [[subtropics|sub-tropical climates]] however, ''Hedychium gardnerianum'' can quickly colonise untended areas. Its sticky seeds are easily spread by birds and roaming mammals,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.asp?ID=4063|title=New Zealand Conservation Network|publisher=New Zealand Conservation Network|access-date=November 13, 2011}}</ref> while rhizomes crowd out native seedlings by forming dense mats. Without human intervention, it can colonise large areas quickly as each rhizome adds at least one segment per season depending on climatic and light conditions.

The methods mentioned above may give some control over any particular clump but will not resolve the problem. Each year, ''Hedychium gardnerianum'''s rhizomes increase the surface area of a particular area, whether the flowers are removed or not. Complete removal of the rhizomes or [[herbicide|poisoning]], (usually before flowers are matured), is the only certain way of controlling the plant if it is considered a weed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://weedbusters.co.nz/weed_info/detail.asp?WeedID=40 |title=Weedbusters Weed Information |publisher=New Zealand Biodiversity Dept |access-date=November 13, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114162705/http://weedbusters.co.nz/weed_info/detail.asp?WeedID=40 |archive-date=January 14, 2012 }}</ref> When ''Hedychium gardnerianum'' is particularly virulent, annual follow up is required for some years to prevent re-infestation. Re-infestation may occur from spreading by neighbouring plants, or dormant seeds disturbed by the removal of the original tuber clump as seeds remain viable for 2–4 years. Lifted rhizomes should be removed from site as if left in contact with soil they will restore themselves.

==Medicinal research==
Medicinal research indicates that the plant compound, villosin, in ''Hedychium gardnerianum'' has potent cytotoxicity activity against human small cell [[lung cancer]] cells.<ref>Kumrit I, Suksamrarn A, Meepawpan P, Songsri S, Nuntawong N.; (2010) "Labdane-type diterpenes from Hedychium gardnerianum with potent cytotoxicity against human small cell lung cancer cells." ''Phytother Res.''; 24(7):1009-13.[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19960422]</ref>
